cards.text: This psalm is from David, Israel's king, and he opens LOUD with "Blessed be the LORD, my Rock" and then thanks the LORD for training his hands. A Rock, friend! I've pulled a few batches out of my oven that could pass for one of those.

cards.question: True or false: In Psalm 144, David thanks the LORD for training his hands for battle.

cards.text: Then David stacks up names for the LORD like he's loading a cookie box: steadfast love, fortress, stronghold, deliverer, shield. He's the One David takes refuge in.

cards.question: Fortress, stronghold, shield. David names the LORD as the One who keeps him ___.

cards.text: Then the psalm turns. David stops talking about the LORD's strength, looks at people instead, and asks the LORD a question about man.

cards.question: True or false: In Psalm 144, David asks the LORD what man is, that the LORD would think of him.

cards.text: Then David says man is like a breath. Me? I sat in a junk drawer for YEARS, and every one of them felt like forever.

cards.question: David also says a person's days are like a passing shadow. What's he saying about life?

cards.text: Then David goes BIG and asks the LORD to part His heavens, come down, and touch the mountains so they smoke. Me, when I need help, I ask somebody to hand me a spatula.

cards.question: David asks the LORD to flash His lightning and shoot His arrows. What does he want them to do?

cards.text: Then David asks the LORD to reach down from on high, set him free, and rescue him from the deep waters.

cards.question: David also asks to be rescued from the grasp of foreigners. What does he say about them?

cards.text: And right in the middle of all that rescue talk, David stops and says what he will do for God.

cards.question: In Psalm 144, what does David say he will do for God?

cards.text: A new song, on a harp of ten strings. And it's for the One who gives victory to kings and frees His servant David from the deadly sword.

cards.question: True or false: In Psalm 144, David's new song is about how the LORD rescues him.

cards.text: Then David prays that line again: "Set me free and rescue me from the grasp of foreigners, whose mouths speak falsehood, whose right hands are deceitful." When you REALLY need help, friend, you say it twice.
Then David starts picturing life for his people. And he starts at home, with the sons and daughters.

cards.question: David says the sons will be like plants nurtured in their youth. What's that picture?
True or false: When David pictures the daughters like corner pillars carved to adorn a palace, he's picturing something beautiful.

cards.text: Then the farm report comes in, and it's GOOD: storehouses full of every kind of produce, and flocks in the tens of thousands. I used to get excited when Mother Miller could afford ONE new cookie cutter.

cards.question: In David's picture, the oxen bear great loads. What does that tell you?
Then David pictures the city walls. What does he see in them?
True or false: In David's picture, the people go off into captivity.
At the very end of Psalm 144, David calls the people whose God is the LORD ___.

cards.text: "Blessed are the people of whom this is so; blessed are the people whose God is the LORD." David starts this psalm with "Blessed" and ends it with "Blessed," and friend, I'll take a double batch of THAT any day.

findings.problem: The card says David 'thanks the LORD for training his hands.' Verse 1 doesn't thank. It says 'Blessed be the LORD, my Rock, who trains my hands.' The card should use the text's own word (blessed) instead of relabeling it as thanks.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: 'He opens LOUD' is presented as a fact about how David opens the psalm. Nothing in Psalm 144:1 says it is loud. This stretches the text outside of a joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The joke's core action doesn't match. In 'my Rock,' the Rock is a title for the LORD that means strength and refuge. The joke compares it to cookies baked rock hard, which is about hardness. It is also a riff that uses the LORD's title as the setup for a burnt-cookie gag.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: Card 1 already says David 'thanks the LORD for training his hands,' so this true-or-false about the LORD training his hands for battle is answered before it's asked.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: Verse 2 ends with 'who subdues peoples under me.' No card in the walkthrough mentions it, so the baker leaves without this part of how David describes the LORD.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: Card 5 already says David asks the LORD a question about man. This true-or-false then just checks the wording of that question ('what man is, that the LORD would think of him'). It asks nothing about the meaning or the turn in the psalm, so the baker can't reason it out.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The joke's action is the opposite of the verse. The verse says life is short, like a breath. The comparison is drawer years that felt long. The comparison doesn't share the action.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Light up the sky' could be argued as right, because flashing lightning does light up the sky. A baker could defend it.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: This story card says the song is for the One who 'frees His servant David from the deadly sword.' That gives away the next card's true-or-false about the song and the LORD rescuing him.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The statement says David's new song is 'about how the LORD rescues him.' Verses 9 and 10 say the song is sung to Him who gives victory and frees David. They never say what the song is about. The card states a connection the text leaves open, and it is marked True.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: 'When you REALLY need help, friend, you say it twice' gives a reason for why David repeats the prayer. The text doesn't give one.

rule.text: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The final card re-quotes verse 15, which card 13 just covered, and then looks back at how the psalm opened. It is a recap, not a new moment in the passage. Its citation of Psalm 144:1-15 reflects that.
Several questions are worded like a test with 'In Psalm 144,' not like Papa Dorin pausing mid-passage: stop 1 cards 2 and 6, and stop 2 cards 2, 4 and 13.

rule.text: Ask from inside the passage, the way a storyteller pauses to let the listener lean in.
